newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's UOB looks abroad for expansion.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's UOB looks abroad for expansion.

text.p: Singapore's United Overseas Bank Ltd (UOB) said on Friday it aims to expand into the booming economies of Southeast Asia and increase its fee-based activities to help maintain double-digit growth.

UOB chairman Wee Cho Yaw told Reuters the bank, Singapore's third largest with assets of Singapore $40.6 billion (US$29.0 billion) at the end of 1995, was becoming constrained by its small domestic market and a maturing local economy.
But the economies around Singapore -- Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and China -- were expanding rapidly and needed huge injections of capital for their development.
"In Singapore, our growth will be quite limited," Wee, who is also UOB's chief executive officer, said in an interview. "So we must grow regionally if we are going to continue to expand."
Wee said overseas earnings currently contributed about 28 or 29 percent to group net profit, but he said this was increasing.
"Outside Singapore, we are looking for 30 to 40 percent of profits, but how long it takes to achieve depends very much on the regional economic growth," he said.

Wee said Thursday's announcement of a merger between UOB's two Malaysian units, Chung Khiaw Bank (Malaysia) Bhd and United Overseas Bank (Malaysia) Bhd, was part of its overall strategy to boost its activities in Malaysia.
The new bank, Malaysia's 11th largest in terms of assets, loans and deposits, would have a far larger capital base and would be able to concentrate on profitable fee-based activities.
A similar move, towards corporate and fee-based income, would be repeated elsewhere, he said.
"Hopefully of our profit, 50 percent will (eventually) be from the non-loan activities," he said.
Wee repeated his own recent forecast that UOB's group net profit should grow at a faster rate year-on-year in 1996 than the 11 percent growth it reported in 1995.
UOB made a net profit of S$632.7 million in the year to December 31, 1995, up from S$601.3 million in 1994.
"Barring unforeseen circumstances...our growth should be slightly better," he said.
He said profits in 1997 might be squeezed by a slowdown in the Singapore economy and tough competition for loans.
Wee said UOB also wanted to do more stock broking and had already established businesses in Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines and Hong Kong.
The bank said on Thursday it would shortly set up a joint venture stock broking in Malaysia with investment firm Affin Holdings Bhd.
He said joint ventures and alliances were likely to become increasingly frequent in the banking industry over the next few years, particularly to offer specific financial services.

"There are very many ways alliances could work, possibly on the syndication side...There are many areas alliances could take place provided all sides agree to it. Asia-Pacific needs a lot of funds for infrastructure, for example, for China power stations, Indochina, India.
"There is a lot of potential synergy (in the industry)."
Such alliances could be an attractive alternative to mergers because it would allow banks to avoid complicated restrictions on foreign ownership which varied throughout Asia, he said.
He said UOB might consider regional acquisitions of other banks but said they were difficult in the current environment.
"Mergers would be difficult because we have a restrictions on the ownership of banks," he said.

"It depends on the opportunity. To acquire banks in the region is not simple. There are different regulatory controls. In Malaysia, for example, you can't buy a controlling interest in a bank. That's so in Thailand. Buying a bank is not easy."
